name: How a Paper Is Cited
title: How a Paper Is Cited
answer: A citation is a formal pointer from one work to another, usually an in-text marker plus an entry in a reference list. It can be direct, where the citing paper builds on the cited one, or indirect, where it merely acknowledges prior art. Citation mapping treats each pointer as an edge in a graph, so a paper's role depends on who cites it, where in the text, and why. The site's own library of 135 research papers is a small graph, but the same rules apply to much larger indexes. Scope also covers self-citation, citation counts, and the difference between a citation and a mention that has no reference entry.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Citations run on persistent identifiers and metadata records. A DOI resolves to a landing page, while Crossref, OpenAlex, and Semantic Scholar expose reference lists, author names, venues, and dates in machine-readable form. ORCID helps disambiguate authors, and citation styles such as APA or IEEE determine how the pointer is formatted, not whether it exists. The site's library of 135 research papers and its 12993 extracted claims both depend on stable links back to the original paper.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work of citation mapping starts with parsing a paper's reference list and matching each entry to a canonical record. Matching uses DOI first, then title, author, year, and venue, with fuzzy matching for older or malformed entries. Once matched, each citation becomes an edge, and the citing context can be classified as background, method, comparison, or extension. Analysts then compute counts, co-citation, bibliographic coupling, and network measures, while checking for duplicates and phantom citations. The result is a graph that shows influence and lineage, not just popularity.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk around citations involve copyright, database terms, and attribution. Reference lists are facts, but the surrounding text and abstracts may be protected, so reuse depends on the source and the license. Provenance matters because a citation count is only as good as the metadata behind it, and errors propagate through downstream indexes. Self-citation, citation rings, and coercive citation are known risks that distort maps. On this site, content never links to the Consensus search tool, it links to the original paper, which keeps provenance clear.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Citation mapping is moving toward open metadata, richer context, and better author disambiguation. More publishers deposit reference lists with DOIs, and tools increasingly expose citation intent and location rather than a bare count. Large language models can help extract and classify citations, but they also risk hallucinated references and must be checked against source records. The field is also paying more attention to citation equity, since coverage varies by language, region, and discipline. The likely direction is a more transparent graph where every edge can be traced to a specific paper and a specific claim.
sections.heading: Where it is going
